title: There is and There are
summary: Talk about the existence and location of one or more things.
explanation: Use there is with one thing and there are with more than one thing.
Use a question form to ask whether something exists in a place.
form: There is + singular noun → There is a book on the table.
There are + plural noun → There are two windows in the room.

examples.sentence: There is a bus stop near my house.
There are three students in the room.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There are a chair in the kitchen.
commonMistakes.correct: There is a chair in the kitchen.
commonMistakes.why: Use there is with a singular noun.

questions.explanation: Supermarket is singular, so use there is.

questions.prompt: There ___ two parks in my town.
questions.explanation: Parks is plural, so use there are.

title: Comparatives and Superlatives
summary: Compare people, places and things using -er, more, -est and most.
explanation: Use a comparative to compare two things and a superlative to compare one thing with a whole group.
Short adjectives usually take -er and -est; longer adjectives use more and most.
form: adjective + -er + than → This route is shorter than that one.
the + most + adjective → This is the most useful tool.

examples.sentence: The blue bag is cheaper than the black bag.
That was the most exciting part of the trip.

commonMistakes.why: Do not use more with an adjective that already has the -er form.

questions.prompt: This route is ___ than the old one.
questions.explanation: Use the comparative shorter to compare two routes.

questions.prompt: It is the ___ building in the town.
questions.explanation: Use the superlative tallest for one building in a group.

title: Present Perfect for Experiences
summary: Talk about experiences without saying exactly when they happened.
explanation: Use have or has plus a past participle for experiences that connect to the present.
Use ever in questions and never for a negative experience. Use the past simple when a finished time is stated.
form: Have/has + past participle → She has visited Hue.
Have you ever + past participle? → Have you ever tried scuba diving?

examples.sentence: I have never flown in a helicopter.
Have they ever won a competition?

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have visited Hanoi last year.
commonMistakes.why: Use the past simple with a finished time such as last year.

questions.explanation: Present perfect uses have plus the past participle eaten.
Yesterday is a finished time, so use the past simple visited.

title: Participle Clauses
summary: Make connected ideas more concise with present and past participles.
explanation: A present participle clause can show two actions by the same subject happening together or in sequence.
A past participle clause often gives a passive or completed meaning.
form: Present participle → Walking home, I called my sister.
Past participle → Designed for small spaces, the desk folds away.

examples.sentence: Having finished the report, she sent it to her manager.
Built from recycled materials, the bench is very durable.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Walking to work, the rain started.
commonMistakes.correct: Walking to work, I noticed the rain started.
commonMistakes.why: The implied subject of the participle clause must be the subject of the main clause.

questions.prompt: ___ the instructions, he assembled the shelf.
questions.explanation: Having read shows that he read the instructions before assembling the shelf.

questions.prompt: ___ in 2020, the centre now serves thousands of people.
questions.explanation: Opened gives the completed passive meaning: the centre was opened.

title: Cleft Sentences
summary: Highlight one part of a sentence for contrast or emphasis.
explanation: Cleft sentences divide information into two clauses so the important element receives focus.
It-clefts often use It was or It is; what-clefts begin with what and identify an action or idea.
form: It was + focus + that/who → It was Maya who found the solution.
What + clause + be → What we need is more reliable data.

examples.sentence: It was the timing that caused the problem.
What matters is how the evidence is interpreted.

commonMistakes.incorrect: It was in June when the project began.
commonMistakes.correct: It was in June that the project began.
commonMistakes.why: Use that after the focused time expression in an it-cleft.

questions.prompt: It was the final paragraph ___ changed my opinion.
questions.explanation: Use that to connect the focused noun phrase to the clause.

questions.prompt: What we need ___ a clearer plan.
questions.explanation: The focused idea plan is singular, so use is.

title: Concession and Qualification
summary: Acknowledge limits and opposing views while making a precise argument.
explanation: Although, while and admittedly introduce a concession: information that does not completely change the main claim.
Qualifying adverbs such as arguably, largely and relatively help a writer avoid claims that are too absolute.
form: Although + concession, main claim → Although the sample was small, the pattern is noteworthy.
Qualifier + claim → The approach is arguably more sustainable.

examples.sentence: Admittedly, the proposal is expensive; nevertheless, it may save money later.
The results are broadly consistent with earlier research.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Although the plan is costly, but it is effective.
commonMistakes.correct: Although the plan is costly, it is effective.
commonMistakes.why: Do not use although and but together in the same clause structure.

questions.prompt: ___ the evidence is limited, the conclusion is worth considering.
The findings are ___ consistent with the earlier study.
questions.explanation: Broadly qualifies the claim and avoids suggesting exact agreement.
